title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get. When a low-return business trades at an average multiple, the market is either pricing in a structural margin inflection—or setting a trap for those who confuse cheapness on EBITDA with cheapness on free cash flow.
epigraph.author: Institutional Valuation Desk Maxim

web_blocks.html: With our price-blind business audit locked at CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL and PASS_WITH_WATCH, we now open the market tape as of the November 16, 2026 close [1, 42]. At $54.64 per share, ABM trades within a 52-week range of $36.96–$55.70 [42]. The company commands a $3.20 billion equity market capitalization across 58.61 million outstanding shares [42]. Net debt and lease obligations total approximately $1.77 billion, yielding a $4.97 billion enterprise value [1, 42]. On surface multiples, ABM appears relatively inexpensive [42]. The stock trades at 12.59x forward P/E and 9.19x EV/EBITDA [42]. Valuation also screens at 0.54x EV/Sales and 10.25x P/FCF with a 2.12% dividend yield [42]. The $1.16 annualized payout reflects a 58-year dividend-increase streak [42]. However, trailing GAAP P/E sits at 19.74x on $2.77 in TTM EPS [42]. This wide 7.15-turn spread between GAAP results and forward expectations warrants careful forensic inspection.

Why does the market price ABM at a $4.97 billion enterprise value [1, 42]? This multiple trails engineering peers like EMCOR Group (12.77x EV/EBITDA) and Comfort Systems (15.58x EV/EBITDA) [43, 44]. Yet it sits above ABM's own historical trough levels [1, 4, 15]. The answer reflects a persistent tug-of-war between two competing market views [1, 15]. The bull thesis emphasizes accelerating portfolio mix shift [10, 11]. Technical Solutions (microgrids via RavenVolt, critical power via Quality Uptime) and Manufacturing & Distribution (cleanrooms via WGNSTAR) generate premium growth and margins [10, 11, 14]. Concurrently, ELEVATE ERP integration expenses are expiring, driving 50.37% TTM EPS expansion as one-off charges fade [16, 42]. In contrast, skeptics emphasize that consolidated ROIC of 4.62% trails ~8.5% WACC [4, 42]. The balance sheet carries $2.59 billion in goodwill, while GAAP operating margin measures only 4.68% [4, 22, 42]. At the same time, Business & Industry (47.2% of sales) remains vulnerable to persistent office vacancies [4, 42].

web_blocks.takeaway: At $54.64, ABM is NOT priced for perfection—it prices in ~3.5% organic growth and ~4.8% operating margins—but meaningful upside to $64+ requires proving that post-ELEVATE FCF (~$280M-$310M) is sustainable rather than a working-capital timing bounce.

web_blocks.caption: ABM Industries vs. Facilities, Uniform & MEP Engineering Peers (Nov 16, 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: ABM trades at the lowest EV/EBITDA (9.19x) and Forward P/E (12.59x) in the peer group, but its 4.62% ROIC explains why the market refuses to award it EMCOR (32.64% ROIC, 12.77x EV/EBITDA) or Comfort Systems (44.06% ROIC, 15.58x EV/EBITDA) multiples.

web_blocks.html: Analyzing the peer group reveals an explicit valuation ceiling [43, 44]. ABM trades at 9.19x EV/EBITDA, while EMCOR Group (EME) commands 12.77x and Comfort Systems (FIX) commands 15.58x [43, 44]. Differing capital efficiency explains this valuation spread [43, 44]. EME generates 32.64% ROIC, while FIX delivers 44.06% ROIC [43, 44]. These specialized mechanical and electrical contractors carry minimal goodwill relative to profits [43, 44]. They also fund operations with negative working capital via project progress billings [43, 44]. In contrast, ABM's 4.62% ROIC aligns closely with asset-heavy service providers [45, 46, 47]. Peers include Aramark (ARMK, 4.85% ROIC, 13.46x EV/EBITDA) and Vestis (VSTS, -0.25% ROIC, 12.35x EV/EBITDA) [45, 46, 47]. ABM trades at a 24% discount to ARMK on forward P/E (12.59x versus 16.53x) [42, 45]. ARMK benefits from higher gross margins and structured food-service pricing escalators [45]. Meanwhile, ABM's commercial office exposure sustains structural investor caution [42, 45].

web_blocks.mechanism: Like ABM, ISS A/S operated a sprawling multi-country janitorial and integrated facility services portfolio weighed down by acquisition goodwill, thin 3–4% operating margins, and a multi-year IT/ERP transformation while office occupancy shifted post-2020.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: ISS de-rated from ~14x EV/EBITDA in 2017 to 7.5x–8.5x EV/EBITDA during 2020–2023 as organic margins stalled near 3.5%–4.3% and FCF conversion disappointed, only re-rating toward ~9.5x–10.5x once net leverage fell below 2.2x and non-core countries were exited.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Low-margin facility integrators rarely re-rate above 10.5x–11.0x EV/EBITDA on revenue growth alone; multiple expansion for ABM to $64+ depends strictly on deleveraging below 2.5x net debt/EBITDA and sustaining >$275M annual free cash flow.

web_blocks.html: Applying a sum-of-the-parts and forward-earnings methodology establishes our independent valuation targets. ABM's 12.59x forward P/E at $54.64 implies ~$4.34 in FY2027E adjusted EPS [42]. Assuming normalized free cash flow of ~$280 million, a modest multiple expansion to 14.7x forward EPS supports our Base Case target of $64.00 (+17.1% upside) [42]. This level equates to ~10.2x EV/EBITDA on ~$550M EBITDA less $1.77B net debt across 58.61M shares [42]. In our Bull Case ($74.00, +35.4%), microgrid backlog and cleanroom staffing lift operating margins toward 5.8% [10, 12]. The market multiple expands to 11.5x EV/EBITDA under this scenario. In our Bear Case ($42.00, -23.1%), office square-footage attrition and wage pressures compress operating margins toward 3.8% [13]. This contraction lowers the multiple to 7.5x EV/EBITDA.

web_blocks.title: Valuation Takeaway: Cheap Enough to Watch, Not Yet Priced for Margin of Safety at 52W Highs
paragraphs: At $54.64, ABM trades 1.9% below its 52-week peak of $55.70 [42]. The stock offers +17.1% upside to our $64.00 Base Case against -14.0% downside to our $47.00 invalidation stop [42]. This setup creates an unappealing 1.23:1 reward-to-risk ratio at current market prices. This asymmetry fails to compensate for a CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL profile generating 4.62% ROIC [42].

A pullback into the $51.36–$53.50 support corridor significantly alters this equation [42]. Upside toward $64.00 expands to +19.6%–24.6% against -8.5% to -12.1% downside risk to $47.00 [42]. This entry zone clears our institutional 1.50:1 asymmetry threshold at a 1.62:1 ratio [42].

web_blocks.caption: EV/EBITDA & Forward P/E Sensitivity Matrix: Implied Equity Value per Share (58.61M Shares, $1.77B Net Debt)
web_blocks.takeaway: Because net debt ($1.77B) represents 35.6% of Enterprise Value, every 1.0x turn of EV/EBITDA moves equity value by roughly $9.40 per share (17%). Deleveraging is therefore a direct equity value catalyst.

web_blocks.html: The valuation sensitivity matrix shows why balance-sheet leverage shapes equity returns [42]. Net debt and lease obligations of $1.77 billion precede the common equity [17, 42]. On $550 million of FY27E EBITDA, every 1.0x move in EV/EBITDA shifts equity value by roughly $9.38 per share [42]. Consequently, debt repayment funded by post-ELEVATE free cash flow compounds equity value even if the multiple stays at 9.2x [24, 42]. Conversely, if office headwinds compress EBITDA to $480 million and the multiple contracts to 8.0x, fair value declines toward $35.30–$42.00 [42].

Across the ten-year valuation cycle, ABM's 9.19x EV/EBITDA sits in the upper half of its historical 7.0x–10.5x range [42]. This valuation reflects optimism that ELEVATE software expenses have peaked [26, 42]. Investors also anticipate durable mid-single-digit growth from Technical Solutions and WGNSTAR cleanrooms [10, 12, 16]. Nevertheless, without a sustainable inflection in ROIC above 8.5%, facility-service economics argue against terminal multiples exceeding 10.5x–11.0x EV/EBITDA.

Dividend investors must balance ABM's 58-year dividend-increase streak against capital-allocation priorities [17, 42]. The dividend yields 2.12% with a $1.16 payout on a 40.93% earnings payout ratio [42]. Annual distributions total ~$68 million, consuming approximately one-quarter of normalized free cash flow [17, 42]. While secure, this ongoing cash commitment reduces surplus funds available for aggressive debt repayment or counter-cyclical share repurchases [17, 42].

What Changes Our Valuation View: Two consecutive quarters of free cash flow exceeding $70M alongside net leverage falling below 2.5x would justify a 10.5x EV/EBITDA re-rating toward $64.00–$74.00 [28, 42]. Conversely, B&I margin compression below 6.0% or annual FCF falling under $180M would confirm our $42.00 Bear Case [1, 24].

book_paragraphs: Now that you and I have completed our price-blind forensic audit of ABM Industries, we can finally open the market tape and ask the question that separates disciplined capital allocators from narrative buyers: what is Mr. Market charging us for this exact set of cash flows today? As of the November 16, 2026 close, ABM trades at $54.64 per share—just 1.9% shy of its 52-week high of $55.70, and nearly 48% above its 52-week low of $36.96.

At first glance, the valuation multiples on your screen look like a value investor's dream. With 58.61 million shares outstanding, ABM's equity market cap is $3.20 billion, and adding roughly $1.77 billion of net debt and lease obligations brings enterprise value to $4.97 billion. Divide that by $9.15 billion of trailing revenue and you get 0.54x EV/Sales. Look at trailing EV/EBITDA of 9.19x, forward P/E of 12.59x, and trailing price-to-free-cash-flow of 10.25x, all paired with a 2.12% dividend yield backed by 58 consecutive years of dividend increases.

But you and I know better than to stop at the headline screener ratios. Whenever a stock trades at 12.59x forward earnings while its trailing GAAP P/E is 19.74x, there is a 7.15-turn wedge between GAAP reality and Wall Street's adjusted consensus. That wedge is where goodwill amortization, ELEVATE ERP transformation expenses, and restructuring charges live. To understand whether $54.64 is a bargain or a value trap, we have to run a Reverse DCF and put ABM side by side with its true industrial peers.

book_subsections.title: What $54.64 Already Assumes: Running the Reverse DCF
paragraphs: When we invert the discounted cash flow model at $4.97 billion of enterprise value using an 8.5% weighted average cost of capital and a 2.5% terminal growth rate, we find that the market is not demanding heroic assumptions. At $54.64, ABM only needs to compound organic revenue at roughly 3.2% to 3.8% per year—right in line with its 3.86% three-year historical sales growth—while holding GAAP operating margins around 4.7% to 5.0% and converting roughly 2.8% to 3.1% of sales into normalized free cash flow ($260 million to $285 million annually).

Notice the catch, though. In FY2025, ABM only generated $155.1 million in free cash flow because ELEVATE ERP investments and working capital ate into operating cash. The trailing twelve-month P/FCF of 10.25x implies that TTM free cash flow surged above $310 million as those ERP outflows tapered and receivables normalized. If that ~$280 million to $310 million FCF run-rate proves durable in FY2027, $54.64 is genuinely inexpensive. If working capital swings back the other way, the apparent 10x cash flow multiple evaporates.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: Always ask why a low-ROIC business looks cheap on forward P/E. A 4.62% ROIC business cannot compound intrinsic value rapidly on retained capital alone; it can only create outsized shareholder returns if it either divests low-return assets, pays down debt aggressively, or shifts its revenue mix toward higher-return technical verticals.

book_subsections.title: The Peer Reality Check: Why ABM Is Not EMCOR or Comfort Systems
paragraphs: If you look at the peer comparison table, you immediately see why institutional investors refuse to pay 15x EBITDA for ABM. EMCOR Group trades at 12.77x EV/EBITDA and Comfort Systems trades at 15.58x EV/EBITDA, and both are compounding machine-like returns on invested capital: 32.64% ROIC at EMCOR and 44.06% ROIC at Comfort Systems. Those businesses don't carry $2.59 billion of janitorial acquisition goodwill on their books, and their specialized mechanical and electrical contracting work commands real pricing power.

ABM's 4.62% ROIC places it in a completely different neighborhood—much closer to Aramark at 4.85% ROIC or Vestis at -0.25% ROIC. Look at ISS A/S in Europe between 2018 and 2024: like ABM, ISS had global scale in facility services, thin 3.5% to 4.3% margins, heavy goodwill, and an expensive IT overhaul. Until ISS proved it could bring net leverage below 2.2x and stabilize free cash flow, the market capped its multiple at 7.5x to 8.5x EV/EBITDA. That historical base rate tells us ABM's natural valuation ceiling is roughly 10.0x to 11.5x EV/EBITDA—not 15x.

book_subsections.title: Base, Bull, and Bear Valuation Targets
paragraphs: Putting the pieces together, our 12-to-18-month Base Case fair value is $64.00 per share (+17.1% from $54.64), anchored on 14.7x forward adjusted EPS of $4.34 and roughly 10.2x EV/EBITDA as ELEVATE costs roll off and net debt edges lower. Our Bull Case reaches $74.00 (+35.4%) if RavenVolt microgrid demand, Quality Uptime critical power, and WGNSTAR semiconductor cleanroom contracts lift consolidated operating margins toward 5.8% and earn an 11.5x EV/EBITDA re-rating.

Our Bear Case sits at $42.00 (-23.1%), reflecting what happens if commercial office vacancy in Business & Industry accelerates, union wage resets squeeze gross margins, and the multiple compresses back to 7.5x EV/EBITDA. At $54.64, buying today gives you only $9.36 of Base Case upside against $7.64 of downside to a $47.00 structural stop—a 1.23:1 ratio that falls short of our institutional 1.50:1 hurdle. Patience to buy on a pullback to $51.36–$53.50 is where the math turns in our favor.

book_subsections.title: How Leverage Magnifies Every Turn of the Multiple
paragraphs: You and I need to pause on one piece of arithmetic that most retail investors miss when looking at a 9.19x EV/EBITDA stock. ABM's enterprise value is $4.97 billion, of which $3.20 billion is equity and roughly $1.77 billion is net debt and lease liabilities. That means debt accounts for more than 35% of the capital structure. In a business with $550 million of forward EBITDA, every single turn of EV/EBITDA expansion or contraction moves the stock by roughly $9.40 per share—nearly 17% of today's share price.

That cuts both ways. On the positive side, if ABM converts $280 million to $310 million of free cash flow per year now that ELEVATE ERP spending is winding down, and directs even $150 million of that toward paying down debt after funding its $68 million annual dividend, equity value accrues by roughly $2.50 per share per year from deleveraging alone. On the negative side, if office occupancy drops and EBITDA slips to $480 million while the multiple compresses to 8.0x, the same leverage pushes the stock down toward $35 to $42. That is why we demand a wide margin of safety at entry rather than paying up near 52-week highs.

Also look closely at Cintas and Vestis in our peer table. Cintas trades at 28.21x EV/EBITDA and 36.29x forward P/E because its uniform-rental route density produces a 29.95% ROIC with recurring pricing power. Vestis, spun out of Aramark, carries -0.25% ROIC and trades at 12.35x EV/EBITDA on turnaround hopes. ABM sits right in the middle: far healthier than Vestis, with a 58-year dividend streak and real microgrid and semiconductor tailwinds, yet nowhere near the capital efficiency of Cintas, EMCOR, or Comfort Systems. Respecting that ceiling keeps us from overpaying.

book_subsections.title: Why Cheap-Looking Multiples Can Still Trap Impatient Buyers
paragraphs: Every value investor eventually learns the difference between a statistically cheap stock and an economically cheap business. On a Bloomberg or Finviz screen, ABM at 12.59x forward earnings and 10.25x trailing free cash flow looks like an obvious bargain in a market where the average industrial trades north of 20x earnings. Yet if you buy a 4.62% ROIC business at 10x EV/EBITDA right after a 40% six-month rally, you are relying entirely on two things going right at the same time: margins expanding and the market keeping the multiple elevated.

Compare that to buying the exact same business after a 4% to 6% pullback into institutional support. At $51.36 to $53.50, you aren't predicting a miracle—you are paying roughly 11.8x to 12.3x forward earnings for a 58-year dividend payer whose ERP cash drag is rolling off, with a clean technical floor right underneath you. That is the difference between hoping for multiple expansion and demanding a margin of safety.

book_subsections.title: The Dividend Aristocrat Illusion vs. Capital Allocation Reality
paragraphs: One final trap to watch out for in Chapter 7 is the comfort blanket of ABM's 58-year dividend-increase streak. At $1.16 per share, the 2.12% dividend yield looks safe—representing roughly 40.9% of adjusted earnings—and income-oriented funds love the consistency of a payout raised every year since the Johnson administration.

Yet you and I have to look at the opportunity cost of that $68 million annual cash outflow. When a company carries $1.77 billion of net debt and lease liabilities while earning 4.62% ROIC, every dollar paid out in dividends is a dollar that isn't retiring debt or funding organic high-ROIC microgrid capacity. The dividend is a nice stabilizer that puts a floor under the stock during mild pullbacks, but it does not create intrinsic value by itself. True value creation over the next 18 months will come from free cash flow above $280 million paying down the acquisition tab.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Valuation is never just a multiple; it is a margin-of-safety calculation. When a stock has already rallied 40.5% in six months to within 2% of its 52-week high, even a reasonable 12.59x forward P/E leaves very little room for an earnings hiccup.
